https://www.surinenglish.com/malaga/marb.text: A 58-year-old man who was arrested after allegedly fatally stabbing his partner at their home in San Pedro Alcántara had confessed the ... killing to a neighbour, who alerted the authorities.The incident came to light at around 4.15pm on Monday when the 112 Andalucía emergency service received a call reporting a violent assault at a property on Calle Castilla. The caller was the neighbour to whom the suspect had allegedly confessed that he had stabbed his partner during the course of Sunday.Several National Police units and emergency medical teams were sent to the address. Officers found the victim, a 36-year-old trans woman of Venezuelan origin, with serious stab wounds, mainly to the chest. Medical staff could only confirm her death and she was not taken to hospital.Police sources said officers found the 58-year-old suspect inside the property and arrested him. During his arrest, he allegedly again admitted that he was responsible for the killing.Police had been called to the property beforeSUR has learned that it was not the first time police had been called to the property. Residents in the area had reportedly contacted police on previous occasions because of violent arguments and fights between the couple.The case is currently being treated, at least in police terms, as a homicide involving domestic violence rather than a gender-based killing. Sources said this was apparently because the victim had not begun the formal procedure to amend the sex recorded on her official documents.A dark JulyThat said, the killing comes against the backdrop of a particularly deadly July for women in Malaga in the context of gender-based violence.On 7 August, the Ministry of Equality confirmed the killing of Melinda, a 45-year-old Hungarian woman , in Benahavís as a case of gender-based violence. She was found dead on 21 July with two cuts to her neck and her clothes torn. Her former partner was not located and arrested until 10 days later.Following the latest confirmation by the Government Delegation against Gender-Based Violence, six women have now been killed by their partners or former partners in Malaga province in 2026. The daughter of one of the victims also died in the same incident .The figure matches the total recorded for the whole of 2025 , when Malaga reached its highest annual figure since records began in 2003 and had the highest number of such killings among Spanish provinces. That position has been repeated in 2026, with Malaga recording more cases than provinces including Madrid, Barcelona and Valencia.

https://hotair.com/john-s-2/2026/08/21/g.text: Germany Finds a Stash of Weapons in a Forest John Sexton 3:20 PM | August 21, 2026 Gavriil Grigorov, Sputnik, Kremlin Pool Photo via AP Here we go again. German authorities found a stash of weapons hidden in a forest near Berlin. Instead of just collecting them, they rendered the weapons non-functional and left them in place to see who might come to collect them. But no one ever turned up. Nevertheless, the suspicion is that this was part of a planned attack . Advertisement German security services are investigating a plot to conduct a politically motivated attack, possibly directed by a foreign power, that was linked to guns found stashed in a forest on the edge of Berlin, the interior minister said on Friday. While Alexander Dobrindt, the interior minister, was careful not to point a finger at any nation, the news came amid increased fear of destabilizing “hybrid” attacks that European governments have blamed, publicly and privately, on Russia. “This case shows that we are working on the assumption that the risk level is high,” Mr. Dobrindt said at a news conference, noting that he had upgraded the threat level this year to high from abstract. There is a suspect that Germany is interested in talking to but he's currently sitting in a Romanian jail . No one was observed trying to collect the weapons, leading investigators to believe the agent or agents had learned of the cache’s discovery and it was now “dead”. Dobrindt described the suspect in Romania, whose nationality was not disclosed, as a “low-level agent” and noted several other such operatives had ‌been detained so far this year. No one is directly blaming Russia but that seems to be the thinking . Peter Neumann, a professor of security studies at King’s College London, said that if the evidence showed the Kremlin was responsible, the German government would face a difficult balance over what to say publicly and what action to take in response. “On the one hand, you want to make clear that it has consequences so that Putin doesn’t see it as a sign of weakness,” Professor Neumann said of the Russian president, Vladimir V. Putin. “On the other hand, you don’t want to get into a direct conflict with Russia.” Advertisement Yes, and it's just as true that Russia doesn't want to start a war with NATO. So Putin is playing these hybrid warfare games . Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said federal prosecutors were investigating a suspect in Romania over suspicions of espionage and "the preparation of a serious act of violence threatening the state". While refusing to confirm reports of Russian links to the cache, Dobrindt said he could not rule out "the involvement of foreign powers". For months security agencies have warned that Russian intelligence services are planning assassinations in Germany, possibly targeting defence industry executives or opposition figures in exile. Just a couple of weeks ago a drone was found at an airport in Leipzig, Germany . A second drone appears to have hit the nose of a plane taking off but in both cases the detonators were flawed and the plastic explosives bombs failed to go off. Russia was strongly suspected in that case and I speculated that the inoperable bombs may have been intended to be inoperable so they would serve as a warning. Putin can't afford to challenge NATO too directly, but he does want to continue to make himself a threat . Russian President Vladimir Putin could try to test NATO’s resolve with a limited assault on an allied country in the next few years, according to new U.S. intelligence reports that posit possible scenarios ranging from a cyberattack to a small-scale land incursion. The U.S. had previously assessed that Putin wouldn’t provoke a North Atlantic Treaty Organization country while he is still fighting in Ukraine. But that assessment changed earlier this year, the U.S. officials said, as Putin is squeezed in Ukraine and under pressure at home to secure a victory. Kyiv’s drones are inflicting growing damage on both Russia’s army and oil industry, while Putin’s forces are making smaller gains at the front line amid heavy casualties. Advertisement Basically, Russia wants to carry out attacks with enough plausible deniability that NATO won't be forced to team up and punch back. At the same time, he wants those European countries to know that it was him so they'll reconsider their support for Ukraine. It's a fine line to walk and he's failed to walk it very well in the past. But these are clear signs that he's getting a bit desperate as the situation in Russia gets more dire thanks to the onslaught of Ukrainian drone attacks. https://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/archae.text: Archaeology reveals new clues about Süleyman’s final campaign News Arts & Life September 09 2026 09:03:06 Archaeology reveals new clues about Süleyman’s final campaign Research in 2024 and 2025 found Ottoman-era artifacts scattered across 80 hectares, shedding light on the settlement known as Turbek. Archaeological research near Szigetvar Castle in Hungary , where Ottoman Sultan Süleyman the Magnificent led his final military campaign, has revealed that the settlement around his presumed place of death was larger than previously thought. Research by the University of Pecs in 2024 and 2025 found Ottoman-era artifacts scattered across approximately 80 hectares, shedding light on the settlement known as Turbek. The findings indicate that Turbek was not only more extensive than earlier estimates suggested but also prosperous. Süleyman left Istanbul on May 1, 1566, to lead his 13th and final military campaign. His imperial tent was erected on a hill overlooking Szigetvar Castle. He died there during the night of Sept. 6-7, 1566, while Ottoman forces were besieging the fortress. Historical sources say his death was concealed from the army to protect morale and ensure the peaceful accession of his son, Selim II. His internal organs were reportedly buried at the encampment, while his body was taken to Istanbul about 42 days later. On Selim II’s orders, a tomb was built at the site where Süleyman was believed to have died. The site later became an important pilgrimage center, with a mosque, dervish lodge, guesthouse and guard barracks nearby. A civilian settlement gradually developed around the complex and became known as Turbek. The settlement was destroyed after Ottoman rule ended, and its location was eventually forgotten. An interdisciplinary team led by Professor Norbert Pap of the University of Pecs examined historical documents, maps and land records. Researchers concluded that the complex stood on Vineyard Hill in the Turbek-Zsibot area, about 4.2 kilometers northeast of Szigetvar Castle. During the 2024-2025 research, Turkish and Hungarian researchers conducted surface studies and geophysical surveys across the wider area. They discovered ceramics, coins, jewelry, Ottoman metalwork, painted glass and porcelain fragments. A rare 16th-century gold coin and a silver coin from the Crimean Khanate were also found. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: An extreme weather survivors meeting in Kerrville, Texas. Photograph: Brenda Bazan/The Guardian View image in fullscreen An extreme weather survivors meeting in Kerrville, Texas. Photograph: Brenda Bazan/The Guardian Texas US extreme weather survivors are a growing group – now they want to be a political force At a gathering in Texas, near where floods killed 136 people last year, survivors are united on the need for urgent action Oliver Milman in Kerrville, Texas Wed 21 Oct 2026 06.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google It may be a club none of its members actually want to be in, but the growing number of people in the US affected by extreme weather disasters are starting to organize into a political force. Severe wildfires, floods storms and other calamities now touch the lives of huge numbers of Americans – about half of all people in the US by one estimate – as the climate crisis supercharges extreme events. Some survivors are now coalescing to push for improved disaster response and even action on the politically contentious issue of global heating. “The group has grown, sadly, quite rapidly,” said Sierra Kos, a film-maker who co-founded Extreme Weather Survivors after being caught in a pall of toxic smoke from wildfires in rural Oregon in 2020 as she attempted to take her son to receive medical care. “I am positive though that survivors of extreme weather will not just shape political outcomes and policies moving forward but also look to run for office,” said Kos. “This is going to be a constituency that policymakers and politicians need to listen to.” View image in fullscreen A charred vehicle in the parking lot of the burned Oak Park Motel after the Santiam fire in Gates, Oregon, in September 2020. Photograph: Kathryn Elsesser/AFP/Getty Images The shock of extreme weather help bonds people in an unusually bipartisan way, Kos said, with politically diverse delegations of survivors making several trips to press lawmakers in Washington. Survivors overwhelmingly feel that the Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) should be more responsive but also that disaster aid should not be politicized, Kos said. Donald Trump has enacted deep cuts to Fema, stressing that states should take more responsibility for disaster relief, and has been accused of withholding resources from states that did not vote for him. “I think you’d be hard pressed to find a group of people that are more united on the core issues,” Kos said of her organization’s survivor network, which now spans around 2,500 people across the US. A meeting of survivors this month in Texas , though, suggests that politicians don’t yet feel overwhelming political pressure to engage with those affected by extreme weather. In a community hall in Kerrville, near where flash floods killed 136 people in 2025, all of the Texas gubernatorial and senate candidates were invited to speak to survivors but only one, Vikki Goodwin, Democratic candidate for lieutenant-governor, showed up. View image in fullscreen Texas state representative Vikki Goodwin speaks with reporters in Kerrville. Photograph: Brenda Bazán/The Guardian “We are seeing more extreme weather in Texas and we need to do more for survivors,” Goodwin told the group. Several of those who spoke at the event expressed surprise at how they had been thrust into the role of advocate. “I just didn’t care about politics. I never thought I’d be doing this,” said Kylie Nidever, a former pre-school teacher whose childhood home in Hunt, Texas, was one of the few in the neighborhood to survive inundation from the floods. “It radicalized me to see my community devastated, and there was some survivors’ guilt, too. So that was initially how I dealt with the trauma,” said Nidever, who has spoken to a committee of Texas lawmakers and expressed shock at the lack of Fema response to similar, less deadly, floods that hit the region again this year . “We need more authority, we need more guidance, we need more support,” she said. “And seeing that not happen even after this second flood has lit a fire under me. I guess I knew it would flood again, I just didn’t think it would happen so soon.” Georgia Bishop, whose best friend Felicity Jarmon died in the 2025 floods, said she still finds it difficult to talk about the disaster, which caused “devastating” damage to her own home. But the 19-year-old has got involved with Extreme Weather Survivors events and traveled to Washington in June to speak to members of Congress about the need for better flood warnings, such as sirens, for communities like hers. View image in fullscreen Flood survivor Georgia Bishop. Photograph: Brenda Bazan/The Guardian The reception she got was mixed, she said, with some lawmakers appearing uninterested while some promised to do more. “My only thing is that you say you’re trying, you say you’re working, and I will believe you on that, but will it be in time before something really is going to happen again?” Bishop said. “I just want to help make sure that this never happens again, because I never want that to happen again to anybody.” Survivor groups routinely share tales of frustration when dealing with the labyrinthine and often fruitless process of dealing with insurance companies, Fema and a catalogue of other local, state and federal government agencies to get the resources to piece back together shattered homes and lives. Several people at the Texas meeting spoke of how they will soon be evicted from temporary housing, with no payments from Fema or other bodies to help make their ruined homes habitable again. Other survivors have been rejected multiple times for Fema assistance, under this and previous administrations. “Fema is terrible, they are awful, they are so inefficient and antiquated that people give up, it’s not worth your stress,” said Elisabeth Anderson, whose home in Atlanta, Georgia was hit by Hurricane Helene in 2025. After several rejected applications, Anderson had to take out a loan to cover the $400,000 needed to repair her home from flooding that had forced her, her husband, child and two dogs to sit on the top of their car to escape the rising waters. “It was insane, like something out of a movie,” she said of the floodwater. “I definitely thought we’d die at one point.” Many survivors complain about the lack of preparation and response to major disasters, Kos said. “There’s this sense of ‘we are American, we should have the best possible evacuation notifications’ – and the fact that all of that funding has been cut really infuriates people,” she added. View image in fullscreen A destroyed motor home sits on the riverbank in Louise Hays Park next to the Guadalupe River in Kerrville in July 2025. Heavy rainfall caused flooding along the Guadalupe River in central Texas with multiple fatalities reported. Photograph: Jim Vondruska/Getty Images These common woes help pull together survivors from different parts of America’s politically fractured landscape, even helping foster a greater appreciation of the role of the climate crisis in disasters among those previously skeptical of such links. Scientists have been clear that global heating likely worsened the floods in Texas and elsewhere, as well as recent heatwaves and wildfires . “I used to think global warming was just indoctrination, then I lived through a flood where I genuinely thought I was going to die,” said Mike Malcolm, a 70-year-old Republican voter from Leander, Texas, who wrote his social security number on his hands and feet in case his body had to be identified as muddy water from the 2025 floods filled his home. Malcolm’s children helped him understand the link between the floods and global heating, he said. “We have to be willing to have difficult conversations and look for solutions,” he added. “I keep asking myself: what do we want to teach our children, and what kind of future do we want to leave them?” View image in fullscreen Flood survivor Kylie Nidever poses for a portrait. Photograph: Brenda Bazan/The Guardian Still, the political toxicity around climate change, which Trump has called a “hoax” and “bullshit”, means that the “C” word is not prominent in survivors groups, sporting names such as Extreme Weather Survivors and Rebuild: the National Disaster Survivors Association . “It’s crazy to me that the term climate change can be divisive, but it can be,” said Nidever. “That’s why we just say extreme weather. We use that instead of going there with climate because it’s more inclusive and it’s not a hot-button term.” Campaigns for the upcoming midterm elections have barely featured mentions of the climate crisis or major disasters, despite American voters wanting politicians to speak more about these issues in the wake of the hottest summer on record in the US and the onset of one of the strongest ever El Niño events , which is already bringing flooding to the west coast and is set to spur even worse heat next year. Survivors may not make a major impact at this election but many feel this will change as warping weather continues to raise home insurance rates and other costs and pockmark large chunks of the year with toxic wildfire smoke, flooding and heat. View image in fullscreen Roberto Marquez continues building a memorial to honor the victims of the Hill Country floods. Photograph: Houston Chronicle/Hearst Newspapers/Getty Images “More and more people know someone affected by this. I was in shock when this happened to me again but I’m not the only one affected by multiple events,” said Alex Webber, a medical journal illustrator who evacuated New Orleans after Hurricane Katrina hit in 2005, only to relocate to Asheville, North Carolina ahead of Hurricane Helene, which tore through the city two years ago . “The money for the region from Fema just hasn’t showed up,” said Webber, who said much of Asheville remains moribund two years after the flooding. “A lot of politicians were paraded downtown, it was like disaster tourism and we felt like zoo animals. Then they disappeared and we are just old news now. “You can’t combat climate change unless you accept it exists; it feels our pigeons are clearly coming home to roost. We can’t keep delaying. We have to solve this, it has to stop being a partisan issue. But there’s nowhere safe now.
